newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's split conservatives contemplate fate.
newsitem.headline: Canada's split conservatives contemplate fate.

text.p: Many conservative Canadians are pleading for cooperation between Canada's two rightist parties to break the dominance of the ruling Liberals, but so much bad blood has been spilled that such an alliance is unlikely.
"I wouldn't allow it to happen," declared Conservative leader Jean Charest on Thursday night.

"I could not look my children in the face at the end of my political career if I accepted that compromise, and don't think there is a Progressive Conservative in the country that would also accept it, and for that reason, there will never be a merger," Charest said.

The Liberals won the federal election last Monday with a majority of just five seats in Canada's 301-seat House of Commons, on 4.93 million votes. Reform won 60 seats and became the official opposition and the Conservatives took 20, on a combined vote of 4.92 million.

Reform is to the right of the Conservatives on social issues such as homosexual rights, while on fiscal policy the Conservative Party ran to the left even of the Liberals in impoverished Atlantic Canada where it won most of its seats.
But the biggest rift between the Conservatives and Reform involves national unity and the vexed issue of Quebec's aspirations to break away from Canada.
Asserting the growing power of the Western provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, Reform Party leader Preston Manning has demanded that the west's voice be heard on the Quebec issue.

He ran a controversial ad during the campaign saying it was time for all Canadians, not just Quebec politicians, to have a say in how to deal with Quebec separatists. That prompted Charest, a francophone Quebecker, to call Manning a bigot.

Yet some Conservatives as well as some of their rivals in Reform are citing the split in the right-wing vote, which allowed another Liberal majority in Monday's election, as a reason for some form of opposition alliance.

The Liberals swept all but two of 103 seats in the electoral treasure-trove of Ontario, partly because of that split, although the combined vote for the Conservatives and Reform was greater than the Liberal vote in 29 electoral districts in the province.

"We're open to suggestions particularly from the grassroots level as to ways to get a single alternative the next time in Ontario," Manning told a news conference on Friday. "I've not much hope for reconciliation at the higher levels of the parties."
He said that local Conservative and Reform organizations might want to propose joint meetings, possibly leading to agreements on proposing a single candidate.
"We're open to the discussion, but so far the federal Tory (Conservative) leadership has tried to squelch it," Manning said.
The idea has the backing of Ontario Premier Mike Harris, a Conservative elected in 1995 after Reform shunned provincial politics, averting a split in the conservative vote.

"I made my view a couple of years ago that I thought it was in the interest of the parties to see if they could not come together. The election result in Ontario has not pointed out to me any difference for the future," Harris said.
A defeated Conservative candidate for Parliament, British Columbia's Al Horning, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. that cooperation was crucial.

"Some kind of coalition or working alliance is going to have to happen some time, because if we keep up doing what we're doing and splitting the conservative parties, none of the parties are ever going to get there and govern.
